doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Studio pay, long days and the studio clique; the chicks
summary: Rates of about 250 dollars for three hours, eight-hour day at Phillips studio, Mottola and Bucky's locker amps, and the chicks guitar rhythm.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: How much did those, what was the studio rate at that time?
On their studio rate I think about two-fifty, about two hundred and fifty dollars, for three hours.

Two-fifty for three. And then it went up and a lot of times of course you went overtime. And that was at Phillips Recording Studio which Bob Crewe was the producer I remember that. We did eight hours one day, I remember that, doing eight hours.
It was a long day. That was a long day.
Did you ever get in a situation where they said okay we’re going to have to go over and you’ve got another gig to get to?
Oh well they probably have, I don’t recall any but I would have to leave.

Yes. Or whoever, there were so many others that had to leave too. Especially Tony Mottola and Bucky, they would have, they would go studio to studio. They would get done with one session at one o’clock and two o’clock started another session at another studio. And they had amplifiers put in lockers. They all chipped in and bought amplifiers, they were the only ones that could use them. So I’d always bring my own amp. I wasn’t in the clique in those days.
And they would just take it out of the locker, boom they were ready. They were ready to play. It was good days. And we were talking about the chicks, like you were saying with

the guitars. One guitar player would just play the chicks on a two and four, and there wasn’t any changes involved. That was playing the high string, and you could hear that. And again if you said to somebody “can you hear the guitar?” “I don’t hear a guitar.” But he’s right there with the chicks. That was very big in the fifties and sixties. And then that went out and then of course they brought the strings in with the rock & roll and all of that, and that sort of went out now too. Now it’s all —
